CNBC, 25 Nov

Crude oil prices rose on Wednesday after Yemen's Houthis said they had attacked Saudi ‌Arabia's largest oil refinery and traders weighed Middle East supply disruptions against the prospect of a global market surplus.

Brent crude futures rose 3.5% to close at $94.61 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures climbed 2% to settle at $83.68. Both benchmarks gained more ​than 2% on Tuesday.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Wednesday that they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery and ​Riyadh's financial district. The refinery, Saudi Arabia's largest, is part of a complex that also serves as ⁠a major export terminal for Saudi crude.

The Houthi statement triggered Wednesday's price rally, said PVM oil analyst Tamas Varga, citing a ​rising geopolitical risk premium.

Traders are also likely to be covering short positions ahead of the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday, which could add ​to the momentum, Varga said.

U.S. crude inventories rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20, data from Energy Information Administration showed. That compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for a 1.5 million-barrel rise.

The build in crude stocks ​was mainly due to weaker crude exports while imports rose, said Bob Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho.

Prices also drew ​support from uncertainty about OPEC's 2027 policies ahead of its November 29 meeting, especially with the United Arab Emirates no longer restricted by OPEC+ policies ‌and Iraq ⁠seeking higher oil output capacity, said Zhenqiang Seto, an oil research specialist at LSEG.

OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide on their 2027 output policy.

"Since the release of an IEA report this month, perceptions of a global supply glut have kept prices in check," said Tsuyoshi Ueno, senior economist at NLI Research Institute. Attention is also focused on how next ​year's production quotas will be ​determined at the OPEC+ meeting, ⁠Ueno added.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said OPEC+ is set to complete a review by year end of member production capacities. Iraq and Kazakhstan were pressing OPEC+ to raise its estimate of their oil ​production capacity, said four people familiar with the matter, heightening tensions over a review that ​will help determine ⁠how much members can pump next year.

In other supply news, Libya's Sharara oil pipeline has reopened. Flows were halted when a valve was closed by what the National Oil Corporation described as an unlawful group. Oil is again flowing into storage tanks at the Akakus facility ⁠in Zawiya, ​NOC said.

In the Strait of Hormuz, a container ship was targeted and came to a ​stop on Tuesday while sailing an "unauthorised" route near the strait, Iran's Revolutionary Guards told state media.
